topics.title: What is accounting? Identify, measure, record, communicate

learn.hook: Every single UPI payment at a college canteen leaves a trail. Accounting is the art of turning thousands of such trails into one clear story: did the canteen make money this year?
points: Accounting is the process of identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information about an organisation to the people who need it for decisions.
Identifying: deciding which events are financial transactions worth recording. Buying stock is recorded; the owner's friendly chat with a customer is not.
Measuring: expressing every recorded event in money (₹). Only what can be measured in money enters the books.
Recording: writing transactions in date (chronological) order in books of original entry, then classifying them into accounts and summarising them into statements.
Communicating: presenting the summarised information (profit and loss account, balance sheet, reports) to users in a form they can understand and act on.

example.q: Arjun runs a mobile-repair shop. Today (i) he bought spare parts for ₹8,000, (ii) a new competitor opened next door, (iii) he paid shop rent ₹5,000. Which events enter his books, and at what value?
steps: Ask: does the event change the business's financial position and can it be measured in money?
(i) Purchase of spare parts: yes, measured at ₹8,000.
(ii) A competitor opening: important, but no money value changes hands, so it is not recorded.
example.answer: Events (i) and (iii) are recorded, ₹13,000 in all; event (ii) is not recorded.

learn.reallife: Indian Railways handles crores of rupees of ticket sales every day. Its accountants identify each sale, measure it in rupees, record it, and finally communicate the yearly results to Parliament and the public.

games.title: The accounting process
games.prompt: Arrange the activities of accounting in the order they happen

Measuring it in money
Recording it in the books

quiz.q: Which activity of accounting answers the question 'Is this event a financial transaction that should be recorded?'
quiz.explain: Identifying means picking out the events that are financial in nature and relevant to the business.
quiz.mistake: Confuses identifying (selecting events) with measuring (putting a ₹ value on them)

quiz.q: A firm records only events that can be expressed in rupees. Which activity of accounting does this describe?
quiz.explain: Measuring means quantifying business transactions in money; money is the common unit of accounting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks measuring means counting physical units such as kilograms or pieces

quiz.q: Recording in accounting is done in which order?
options: Chronological order, that is, in order of date
Any order, as long as totals agree
quiz.explain: Transactions are entered in books of original entry in the order in which they occur (date-wise).
quiz.mistake: Mixes up recording in the journal with arranging accounts in the ledger

quiz.q: Which is the best description of accounting?
options: Only preparing tax returns for the government
Only checking whether the cash in hand is correct
Identifying, measuring, recording and communicating economic information to users for decisions
quiz.explain: Accounting is a complete process that ends with useful information reaching users; recording alone is only one part.
quiz.mistake: Equates accounting with only one of its stages, such as recording

quiz.q: Sneha's bakery: she bought flour for ₹6,000, paid wages ₹4,000 and hired a new baker who joins next month. What total amount is recorded today?
quiz.explain: Flour purchase and wages paid are transactions. Hiring a baker who has not yet worked or been paid involves no money value today.
quiz.mistake: Records the hiring of an employee as if it were a transaction

quiz.q: The final stage of the accounting process, in which statements reach owners, lenders and others, is called
quiz.explain: Communicating means passing summarised information to users in the form of reports and financial statements.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the process ends once entries are recorded

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The resignation of a firm's best salesperson is not recorded in the books.
Reason (R): Accounting records only events that can be measured in money.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Losing a talented person may hurt the business, but it cannot be measured in rupees, so it is not recorded. R explains A exactly.
quiz.mistake: Assumes every important event must be recorded

quiz.q: Classifying and summarising are carried out mainly after which activity?
quiz.explain: Once transactions are recorded in the journal, they are classified into ledger accounts and summarised into statements.
quiz.mistake: Places summarising before transactions are even recorded

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'My aunt says accounting is just writing numbers in a notebook. Is that all? Teach me the full process!'
teach.praise: Tweet! Identify, measure, record, communicate. Accounting is a whole journey, not just a notebook!
teach.nudge: Good start! After the numbers are written down, who gets to see them, and how?

topics.title: Book-keeping, accounting and the information system

learn.hook: Book-keeping is like scoring every ball in a cricket match. Accounting is the analyst who studies the scorecard and tells the captain why the team lost.
points: Book-keeping is the recording stage: identifying, measuring, recording and classifying transactions. It is routine and largely clerical.
Accounting begins where book-keeping ends: it summarises, analyses and interprets the recorded data and communicates the results.
Book-keeping is the base of accounting; accounting has a wider scope and needs judgement.
Accounting works as an information system: inputs are transactions; processing is recording, classifying and summarising; outputs are financial statements and reports for decision makers.
Because it communicates the financial results of every kind of enterprise in a common form, accounting is called the language of business.

example.q: A shop's clerk writes all sales and purchases into books daily. At year-end, a chartered accountant reads the books and tells the owner that profit fell because of rising transport costs. Which part is book-keeping and which is accounting?
steps: The clerk's daily recording of transactions = book-keeping.
Analysing the books and explaining why profit fell = analysis and interpretation, which belongs to accounting.
Passing the conclusion to the owner = communicating, also accounting.
example.answer: The clerk does book-keeping; the accountant's analysis, interpretation and communication is accounting.

learn.reallife: At a start-up such as a Bengaluru food-delivery firm, software records thousands of orders (book-keeping), while the finance team analyses margins per city to decide where to expand (accounting as an information system).

games.title: Book-keeping or accounting?
items: Writing daily cash sales in the cash book

Interpreting why profit fell this year
Recording a credit purchase in the purchases book

quiz.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes book-keeping from accounting?
options: Book-keeping is the recording stage, while accounting also analyses, interprets and communicates
Book-keeping and accounting mean exactly the same thing
Accounting is a part of book-keeping
Book-keeping needs more judgement than accounting
quiz.explain: Book-keeping is the foundation; accounting is wider and includes analysing and interpreting the recorded data.
quiz.mistake: Treats book-keeping and accounting as identical

quiz.q: Why is accounting called the 'language of business'?
options: It is written only in English
It communicates the financial results of a business to users in a common, understood form
It is used only by lawyers in business disputes
It replaces the need for any spoken communication
quiz.explain: Just as a language passes on ideas, accounting passes on financial information about a business to all interested users.
quiz.mistake: Takes 'language' literally to mean a spoken or written language

quiz.q: In accounting as an information system, financial statements are the
quiz.explain: Transactions are the input, recording and summarising is the processing, and statements and reports are the output.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the raw input (transactions) with the final output

quiz.q: Which task is part of accounting but NOT of book-keeping?
options: Entering cash received in the cash book
Interpreting the results shown by the financial statements
quiz.explain: Recording and posting are book-keeping tasks; interpretation of results is done at the accounting stage.
quiz.mistake: Thinks posting to the ledger is an analytical task

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Book-keeping is the base for accounting.
Reason (R): Accounting cannot analyse data until transactions have been recorded and classified.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Analysis and interpretation need recorded data, which book-keeping provides; so book-keeping is the foundation.
quiz.mistake: Thinks accounting and book-keeping are independent processes

quiz.q: An accounting information system collects, processes and reports data mainly to help
quiz.explain: The whole purpose of the system is decision-useful financial information for users.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that the end purpose of accounting is decision making

quiz.q: Who usually performs book-keeping in a large business?
options: Junior staff or clerks, often using accounting software
quiz.explain: Book-keeping is routine and clerical, so it is done by junior staff or software; analysis needs senior accountants.
quiz.mistake: Assumes routine recording must be done by top officials

quiz.q: A company's software records 5,000 sales a day. What does the processing stage of the accounting information system do with them?
options: Deletes them after the day ends
Sends them directly to customers as bills
quiz.explain: Processing turns raw transactions into organised, summarised data that can be reported.
quiz.mistake: Confuses processing with an unrelated business action

teach.ask: Gappu flaps: 'If a clerk records every sale, why do we still need an accountant? Aren't they the same?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The clerk records; the accountant analyses, interprets and tells users what it means.
teach.nudge: Nice! What does an accountant do with the records that a book-keeper does not?

learn.hook: When a bank like SBI decides whether to lend ₹2 crore to a textile mill in Surat, its credit officer reads one thing first: the mill's financial statements.
points: Internal users work inside the business: owners (is my investment earning?), management (planning, control, decisions) and employees (job security, wages, bonus).
External users are outside the business: investors and potential investors, lenders and banks, suppliers and creditors, government and tax authorities, customers, researchers and the public.
Each user needs different information: lenders need repaying capacity and security; creditors need short-term liquidity; investors need profitability and growth.
Government and tax authorities use accounts to assess tax (income tax, GST) and to frame policy; researchers use them for studies.
Customers want to know that the business will keep supplying goods and honouring warranties.

example.q: Match the user to the information: (i) Punjab National Bank considering a loan, (ii) workers' union negotiating bonus, (iii) a supplier selling on 30-day credit.
steps: (i) A lender wants to know whether the firm can repay principal and pay interest: solvency and repaying capacity.
(ii) Employees want profitability, because bonus and job security depend on profits.
(iii) A trade creditor wants to know whether the firm can pay within a short period: liquidity.
example.answer: Bank: repaying capacity; union: profits for bonus; supplier: short-term liquidity.

learn.reallife: Before a company lists on the NSE or BSE, its audited accounts go into the offer document so that lakhs of retail investors can judge its profitability.

quiz.q: Which user group uses accounting information mainly to assess taxes such as income tax and GST?

quiz.q: Workers of a cement company want a higher bonus. Why would they study the company's accounts?

quiz.explain: Employees use profit figures to argue for bonus and to judge their job security.
quiz.mistake: Does not link bonus to profits

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Potential investors are external users of accounting information.
Reason (R): They do not take part in the internal management of the business.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

quiz.explain: External users are those outside management; potential investors are not yet part of the firm, so they are external.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anyone with money interest is an internal user

quiz.q: Case: Kavya plans to buy shares of a listed company. Which information is most useful for her?
options: The number of holidays employees get
The colour of the company logo
Profitability, growth and the safety of her investment
Only the company's cash in hand on one day
quiz.explain: Investors want to know whether the investment will earn returns and be safe.
quiz.mistake: Picks information that is irrelevant to an investment decision

quiz.q: Customers of a firm that gives long warranties are interested in its accounts because they want to know
options: How much salary the manager gets
Whether the firm will continue to exist and honour its commitments
quiz.explain: Customers want continuity of supply and service, which depends on the firm staying financially sound.
quiz.mistake: Assumes customers have no interest in a firm's accounts

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Who on earth reads a firm's accounts? Just the owner, right?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Owners, managers and workers inside, and banks, investors, suppliers and the government outside. Lots of readers!
teach.nudge: Good! The owner is one user. Who outside the business might read the accounts?

learn.hook: A weather forecast is useless if it arrives after the monsoon storm, or if it is wrong. Accounting information has the same test: is it reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable?
points: Reliability: information must be verifiable, faithfully represent what happened, and be free from error and bias. Independent persons using the same method should reach the same figures.
Relevance: information must reach users in time and help them make decisions; it should have predictive value (helps forecast) or feedback value (confirms or corrects earlier expectations).
Understandability: information must be presented clearly so that users with reasonable business knowledge can understand it.
Comparability: users should be able to compare a firm's results over different periods (inter-period) and with other firms (inter-firm). This needs consistent methods and a common format.
These four characteristics decide how useful accounting information is; missing even one reduces its value.

example.q: A firm changes its method of valuing stock every year without disclosure, so this year's profit cannot be compared with last year's. Which qualitative characteristic is hurt?
steps: Ask: can users compare results across periods?
Changing methods each year breaks inter-period comparison.
So comparability is lost (consistency of methods supports comparability).

learn.reallife: RBI asks all banks to publish results in a common format each quarter, so analysts can compare HDFC Bank with Bank of Baroda: comparability in action.

games.title: Characteristic to its test

games.title: Quality check
items: Information that reaches the manager after the decision is already taken lacks relevance.
Timeliness is part of relevance; late information cannot influence the decision.
Reliable information must be verifiable.
Verifiability is a key part of reliability.
Comparability means a firm must use the same methods as every other firm in the world.
Comparability needs consistent methods and clear disclosure, not identical methods everywhere.
Understandability means statements should be written for users with reasonable business knowledge.
Information is prepared for users who have reasonable knowledge of business and accounting.
Information can be biased and still be reliable.
Reliability requires freedom from bias.
Predictive value is a part of relevance.
Relevant information helps users predict future outcomes.

quiz.q: Accounting information that is verifiable and free from error and bias is said to be
quiz.explain: Reliability means users can depend on the information because it is factual and verifiable.
quiz.mistake: Confuses reliability with relevance

quiz.q: Annual accounts are published 18 months after the year ends. Which characteristic is mainly lost?
quiz.explain: Information must be timely to influence decisions; late information loses relevance even if accurate.
quiz.mistake: Thinks accuracy alone makes information useful

quiz.q: Comparing Tata Motors' profit this year with its profit last year is an example of
quiz.explain: Comparing the same firm over different periods is inter-period comparison.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up inter-period and inter-firm comparison

quiz.q: Why must accounting information be understandable?
options: So that it can be kept secret
So that it never needs to be audited
Users can act only on information they can make sense of
quiz.explain: If users cannot understand the information, it cannot help them decide, however accurate it is.
quiz.mistake: Thinks complex presentation makes information more valuable

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Comparability requires that a firm follow consistent accounting methods over time.
Reason (R): If methods change every year, differences in results may arise from the method rather than from performance.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Consistent methods make year-to-year figures comparable; R gives the reason.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the link between consistency and comparability

quiz.q: Which feature belongs to relevance rather than reliability?
quiz.explain: Relevance covers timeliness, predictive value and feedback value; the other three are parts of reliability.
quiz.mistake: Places verifiability under relevance

quiz.q: Case: Two accountants independently check a firm's records and arrive at the same profit figure. This shows the information is
quiz.explain: When independent persons reach the same result, the information is verifiable and hence reliable.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect verifiability with reliability

quiz.q: How many qualitative characteristics of accounting information are explained in NCERT Class 11?
quiz.explain: They are reliability, relevance, understandability and comparability.
quiz.mistake: Counts only reliability and relevance

teach.ask: Gappu peeps: 'If numbers are written in the books, they are automatically useful, right?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Reliable, relevant, understandable and comparable. Only then is information truly useful!
teach.nudge: Hmm, what if the numbers come too late, or can't be compared with last year? Which qualities are missing?

topics.title: Objectives, role and limitations of accounting

learn.hook: No shopkeeper can remember 10,000 transactions. Accounting is the business's memory, its profit meter and its health report, all rolled into one.
points: Objectives: (1) maintain systematic and complete records of transactions; (2) calculate profit or loss for a period by matching revenues and expenses; (3) show the financial position (assets and liabilities) through a balance sheet; (4) provide information to users for decisions.
Role: accounting is the language of business and a historical record of transactions in date order.
It also reflects current economic reality (how wealthy the business is now), works as an information system and is a service activity that serves decision makers.

Limitations: it ignores non-monetary facts (staff skill, reputation); it records items at historical cost and is affected by changes in price level; it relies on estimates (useful life, bad debts) and on personal judgement in choosing methods.

example.q: Rohan bought a building in 2005 for ₹40 lakh. Today it could sell for ₹2 crore, yet his balance sheet shows it at cost less depreciation. Which limitation of accounting does this show?
steps: The asset is recorded at historical cost, the price paid when acquired.
Its market value has risen because of price-level changes, but books do not show that.
So the balance sheet does not reflect current value.
example.answer: Historical cost and price-level changes make the balance sheet differ from current market values.

learn.reallife: An ISRO vendor in Bengaluru may have world-class engineers, but their talent never appears in the balance sheet, because accounting ignores non-monetary facts.

quiz.q: Which of the following is NOT an objective of accounting?

quiz.q: Which statement shows the financial position of a business on a particular date?

quiz.q: A company has highly loyal, skilled staff, but this is not shown in its accounts. This is because accounting

quiz.explain: Non-monetary facts like staff quality are ignored by accounting, a known limitation.

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Accounting information may not show the current value of assets.
Reason (R): Assets are generally recorded at historical cost.

quiz.q: Which role of accounting highlights that it helps users know the real wealth of a business today?
quiz.explain: As current economic reality, accounting aims to show the present financial state of the business.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up current economic reality with historical record

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'Why do businesses bother with accounting at all? And can accounting ever miss something?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Keep records, find profit, show position, help users. And yes, it can't measure loyalty or price changes!
teach.nudge: Nice! You told me why. Now, is there anything accounting cannot show?

topics.title: Basic terms I: entity, transaction, assets, liabilities, capital

learn.hook: Every business, from a pani-puri stall to Reliance, sits on one simple balance: what it owns equals what it owes to outsiders plus what it owes to its owner.
points: Entity: an organisation with a separate identity, like a shop, firm or company. A business transaction is an exchange of money or money's worth between the business and another party.

Assets: economic resources owned or controlled by the business that will bring future benefit. Non-current assets are held for long-term use (land, building, machinery); current assets are converted to cash within one year or the operating cycle (cash, debtors, stock).

Liabilities: amounts the business owes to outsiders. Non-current liabilities are payable after more than a year (long-term loan); current liabilities are payable within a year (creditors, bills payable, bank overdraft).
Capital: amount invested by the owner. It is the owner's claim on the assets, so Capital = Assets − Liabilities.

example.q: Neha's boutique has cash ₹30,000, stock ₹70,000, furniture ₹50,000, creditors ₹40,000 and a 3-year bank loan ₹60,000. Find her capital.

learn.reallife: A Kochi spice exporter's warehouse (non-current asset), its stock of cardamom (current asset) and its loan from SIDBI (non-current liability) all appear in its balance sheet.

games.title: Current or non-current?
items: Stock of goods is a current asset.
Stock is expected to be sold and turned into cash within the operating cycle.
Building used by the business is a current asset.
A building is held for long-term use, so it is a non-current asset.

options: Purchase of a computer for the office for ₹45,000
Placing an order for goods to be delivered next month
Receiving a quotation from a supplier
quiz.explain: Only the purchase involves an actual exchange of money or money's worth now.
quiz.mistake: Treats an order or appointment as a transaction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Capital is treated as a liability of the business.
Reason (R): The business is separate from its owner and owes the capital to the owner.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because the business entity is separate from the owner, the capital is the owner's claim against the business.
quiz.mistake: Thinks capital is an asset because it is 'money'

quiz.q: A firm's assets: land ₹5,00,000, stock ₹1,50,000, cash ₹50,000. Liabilities: creditors ₹1,00,000. What is the owner's capital?
quiz.explain: Total assets are ₹7,00,000; deducting creditors ₹1,00,000 gives the owner's claim.
quiz.mistake: Stops at total assets and forgets to deduct liabilities

quiz.q: Bank overdraft is classified as a
quiz.explain: An overdraft is money owed to the bank, repayable on demand, so it is a current liability.
quiz.mistake: Thinks anything at the bank is an asset

teach.ask: Gappu blinks: 'My uncle runs a shop. He says the shop owes him money! How can a shop owe its own owner?'
teach.praise: Tweet! The business is a separate entity, so it owes capital to the owner: assets minus liabilities!
teach.nudge: Close! Is the business the same person as the owner in the books? What is capital equal to?

topics.title: Basic terms II: revenue, expense, expenditure, profit, gain, discount

learn.hook: A sweet shop sells ₹1,00,000 of laddoos in Diwali week, gets a 10% trade discount from its supplier and also sells an old fridge at a profit. Are all these 'profit'? Accounting says no.
points: Sales: amount from selling the goods or services the business deals in. Revenue: amounts from regular operations, including sales, commission, interest, rent and dividends received.

Expense: cost used up in earning revenue during the period (rent, wages, depreciation). Expenditure: spending of money or creating a liability; if benefit lasts beyond the year it is capital expenditure (machinery), if within the year it is revenue expenditure.

Profit: excess of revenues over expenses of a period. Gain: profit from incidental or irregular events, such as selling a fixed asset above book value. Loss: excess of expenses over revenue, or money lost without benefit (fire, theft).

Trade discount: reduction in the list price at the time of sale; it is not recorded in the books. Cash discount: allowed for prompt payment; it is recorded (discount allowed is a loss, discount received is a gain).
Net amount after trade discount = List price × (1 − rate). Cash discount is then calculated on this net amount.

example.q: Goods with list price ₹50,000 are sold at 10% trade discount and 2% cash discount for immediate payment. How much cash is received?

learn.reallife: During the Big Billion Days sale, an online seller offers lower prices on MRP (trade discount) and an extra 'instant bank discount' for paying immediately with a card (similar to a cash discount for prompt payment).

games.title: Term to meaning
pairs: Profit on sale of an old machine
Cost used up in earning revenue
Reduction in list price, not recorded

items.q: Old car: book value ₹1,00,000, sold for ₹1,20,000. Gain?
Invoice ₹50,000 less 1% cash discount. Cash received?

quiz.q: Goods of list price ₹80,000 are sold at 15% trade discount. What amount is recorded as sales?
quiz.explain: Trade discount is deducted on the invoice itself and is not recorded, so sales are recorded at the net amount.
quiz.mistake: Records sales at list price and shows trade discount separately

quiz.q: Goods listed at ₹30,000 are sold at 10% trade discount and 5% cash discount, the buyer paying at once. What is the cash discount?
quiz.explain: Cash discount is computed on the amount after trade discount.
quiz.mistake: Calculates cash discount on the list price

quiz.q: Which of these is a gain rather than revenue?
options: Sale of goods by a trader
Profit on the sale of an old delivery van
quiz.explain: A gain arises from incidental events like selling a fixed asset; the others come from regular operations.
quiz.mistake: Treats all profits as revenue

quiz.q: Why is trade discount not recorded in the books of accounts?
options: Because it is always very small
Because it is recorded only by the government
It is deducted from the list price on the invoice itself, so only the net amount is the transaction value
quiz.explain: The transaction takes place at the net price; the list price is never the actual exchange value.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every discount must be recorded

quiz.q: Expenditure on buying a machine that will be used for 10 years is
options: An expense of the current year only
quiz.explain: Its benefit lasts beyond one year, so it is capital expenditure; only its depreciation becomes an expense each year.
quiz.mistake: Treats all expenditure as an expense of the year

quiz.q: A firm earned revenue of ₹6,50,000 and incurred expenses of ₹7,10,000. What is the result?
quiz.explain: Expenses exceed revenue, so the firm suffers a loss of ₹60,000.
quiz.mistake: Adds revenue and expenses

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Cash discount allowed is recorded in the books of the seller.
Reason (R): Cash discount is allowed on the list price before the invoice is prepared.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Cash discount is recorded as a loss for the seller, but it is allowed at the time of payment on the invoice amount, not on the list price.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the timing and base of cash and trade discount

quiz.q: Which pair correctly distinguishes expense from expenditure?
options: Expense is always cash; expenditure is always credit
Expense is capital; expenditure is revenue
Expense is the cost used up in earning revenue of a period; expenditure is spending whose benefit may last longer
quiz.explain: All expenses arise from expenditure, but not all expenditure becomes this year's expense.
quiz.mistake: Treats the two words as synonyms

teach.ask: Gappu squawks: 'My cousin got 10% off on MRP and 2% off for paying cash. Are both discounts written in the shop's books?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Trade discount is off the list price and never recorded; cash discount is for prompt payment and is recorded!
teach.nudge: Good! But which discount is recorded, and which one never appears in the books?

topics.title: Basic terms III: voucher, goods, purchases, stock, drawings, debtors, creditors

learn.hook: When a kirana owner takes a packet of tea home for the family, that tiny act has a name in accounting, and it reduces his capital.
points: Voucher: documentary evidence supporting a transaction, such as a cash memo, invoice, receipt or salary slip.
Goods: items the business buys and sells as its regular activity. Furniture is goods for a furniture dealer but an asset for a lawyer.

Purchases: goods bought for resale or for production, either for cash or on credit. Stock (inventory): goods unsold on a date. Opening stock is at the start of the period; closing stock is at the end.
Drawings: cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use. Drawings reduce capital.
Debtors: persons or entities who owe money to the business, usually from credit sales. Creditors: persons or entities to whom the business owes money, usually for credit purchases.

example.q: A cycle dealer starts the year with stock ₹40,000, buys cycles worth ₹1,60,000, and at year-end has stock worth ₹30,000. What is the cost of cycles sold?
steps: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock.

learn.reallife: A Ludhiana hosiery wholesaler sells to hundreds of retailers on credit. Those retailers are its debtors, and the yarn mills it buys from on credit are its creditors.

games.title: Goods or asset?
items: Laptops for a laptop dealer
A laptop used by a lawyer
Cars for a car showroom
Delivery van of a grocery shop
Furniture for a furniture dealer
Furniture in a doctor's clinic

quiz.q: A furniture dealer buys tables to resell. For him, these tables are
quiz.explain: Items bought for resale in the regular course of business are goods for that business.
quiz.mistake: Classifies items by their nature (furniture) instead of their purpose

quiz.q: The owner withdraws goods costing ₹3,000 for personal use. This is
quiz.explain: Any cash or goods withdrawn by the owner for personal use is drawings, which reduces capital.
quiz.mistake: Treats goods taken by the owner as a sale

quiz.q: A person to whom the business owes money for goods bought on credit is a
quiz.explain: Creditors are those to whom the business owes money.
quiz.mistake: Swaps debtors and creditors

quiz.q: Opening stock ₹25,000, purchases ₹1,75,000, closing stock ₹40,000. What is the cost of goods sold?
quiz.explain: Cost of goods sold = Opening stock + Purchases − Closing stock.
quiz.mistake: Adds closing stock instead of subtracting it

quiz.q: A firm's capital was ₹2,00,000. The owner withdrew ₹15,000 for personal use and the firm earned a profit of ₹35,000. What is the closing capital?
quiz.explain: Profit increases capital and drawings reduce it.
quiz.mistake: Adds drawings to capital

quiz.q: Which document is an example of a voucher?
options: A cash memo issued for a cash sale
A price list sent to customers
quiz.explain: A voucher is documentary evidence of a transaction that has taken place; a cash memo proves a cash sale.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any business document is a voucher

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Purchases include both cash and credit purchases of goods.
Reason (R): Purchases means buying only fixed assets for the business.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Purchases are goods bought for resale or production, whether for cash or on credit. Buying fixed assets is not 'purchases' in accounting.
quiz.mistake: Thinks buying furniture or machinery counts as purchases

quiz.q: Total credit sales ₹3,00,000; cash received from these customers ₹2,20,000. What is the amount of debtors at the end?
quiz.explain: Debtors are customers who still owe the business.
quiz.mistake: Takes cash received as the debtors balance

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'A shopkeeper took a box of biscuits home. He says it is drawings. Isn't drawing about pictures?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Drawings are cash or goods the owner takes for personal use, and they reduce capital. No crayons involved!
teach.nudge: Good! Who takes the goods, and for what use? What happens to capital then?
